# Install

There are up to three things to install: the Python library (always), the headset app (once per headset), and the
desktop client (optional, for trying a server without a headset).

## Requirements

| What | Needed for |
|---|---|
| Python 3.10 or newer, pip | the library, the demo, the probe |
| numpy | the library (installed automatically) |
| git | cloning the repository to build the headset app or the desktop client |
| Linux on x86-64 | the build scripts (`android/setup_toolchain.sh` downloads the Linux Android tools) |
| cmake 3.18 or newer, make, curl, unzip, zip | building the APK |
| a Java runtime, version 17 or newer | `sdkmanager`, `apksigner` and `keytool` while building the APK |
| about 2.5 GB of disk | the Android SDK tools, the NDK and the OpenXR loader |
| a Meta Quest headset (tested on a Quest 2) in developer mode | running the app |
| a USB-C data cable | installing the app on the headset |

On Debian or Ubuntu, for example:

```bash
sudo apt install git python3-pip cmake make curl unzip zip openjdk-17-jdk-headless
```

## 1. The Python library

```bash
pip install git+https://github.com/EntangledQuantum/quest-teleop
```

Or from a clone:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/EntangledQuantum/quest-teleop.git
cd quest-teleop
pip install .            # or: pip install -e .   (editable, for working on the library)
```

This installs the `quest_teleop` package (its only dependency is numpy) and two commands:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `quest-teleop-demo` | the bundled demo server with a mock world, the status page and recording ([Quick start](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/quick-start.md)) |
| `quest-teleop-probe` | a headless Python client: checks a server and measures latency and bandwidth |

Check it:

```bash
python -c "import quest_teleop; print(quest_teleop.__version__)"     # 0.2.0
quest-teleop-demo --help
```

## 2. The headset app

The app is built from the repository with two scripts. No Android Studio, no Gradle, no Java sources: NDK clang
through CMake builds one shared library, then `aapt2`, `zip`, `zipalign` and `apksigner` package and sign it with a
debug key.

### 2.1 Install the Android toolchain (once)

```bash
git clone https://github.com/EntangledQuantum/quest-teleop.git     # if you have not cloned it yet
cd quest-teleop
android/setup_toolchain.sh
```

It installs into `~/android-sdk` (set `ANDROID_HOME` to choose another folder), about 2.4 GB:

| Component | Version |
|---|---|
| Android command-line tools | 11076708 |
| platform-tools (`adb`) | latest |
| build-tools (`aapt2`, `zipalign`, `apksigner`) | 34.0.0 |
| platform (`android.jar`) | android-32 (the APK targets API 32; its minimum is API 29) |
| NDK | 27.2.12479018 (r27c) |
| Khronos OpenXR loader for Android | 1.1.65 |

It downloads only from `dl.google.com` and `github.com/KhronosGroup`. **Running it accepts the Android SDK licence
agreements** (`sdkmanager --licenses`); an agent should tell the user this before running it. Running it again is
safe: finished parts are skipped.

At the end it prints where `adb` is: `~/android-sdk/platform-tools/adb`. The other pages write plain `adb`; either
put that folder on your `PATH` or use the full path:

```bash
export PATH="$HOME/android-sdk/platform-tools:$PATH"
```

### 2.2 Build the APK

```bash
android/build_apk.sh            # builds build/quest-teleop.apk (about 1 MB)
```

The APK is signed with the standard Android debug key in `~/.android/debug.keystore` (created with `keytool` if it
is missing). That is all a sideloaded developer build needs.

### 2.3 Install it on the headset

The headset must be in developer mode, connected by USB, and listed by `adb devices` as `device`: see
[Headset setup](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/quest-setup.md) first. Then:

```bash
android/build_apk.sh install    # builds, runs `adb install -r build/quest-teleop.apk`, and starts the app
```

To start the app with a fixed server address instead of finding the server by itself:

```bash
SERVER=192.168.1.20 android/build_apk.sh install
```

An APK that is already built installs with plain adb:

```bash
adb install -r build/quest-teleop.apk
```

In the headset the app is under **Library**, filter **Unknown sources**; its label there is **Quest Teleop**. Its package name is
`com.entangledquantum.questteleop`.

## 3. The desktop client (optional)

The same C++ core as the headset app, in an X11 window. Needs a C++17 compiler and the X11, EGL, OpenGL ES and zlib
development files:

```bash
sudo apt install g++ cmake make libx11-dev libegl-dev libgles-dev zlib1g-dev     # Debian / Ubuntu
cmake -S client -B build/desktop && cmake --build build/desktop -j
build/desktop/qt_desktop                     # finds the server by broadcast
build/desktop/qt_desktop --server 127.0.0.1  # or: a given address, HOST[:PORT]
```

Options: `--server HOST[:PORT]`, `--tcp-only` (tunnel everything through TCP), `--size WxH`. The controls are on the
[Quick start](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/quick-start.md#4-desktop-client-controls) page.

## 4. Run the tests (optional)

In a clone:

```bash
pip install pytest
python -m pytest -q
```

They cover protocol round trips, the server and the probe over loopback, recovery from packet loss, recording and
the status page.

## Uninstall

```bash
pip uninstall quest-teleop
adb uninstall com.entangledquantum.questteleop
```

The toolchain is the folder `~/android-sdk` (or your `ANDROID_HOME`); delete it by hand only if nothing else uses
it.

Next: [Headset setup](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/quest-setup.md).


---

<!-- page: https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/quest-setup.md -->

# Headset setup

What the headset needs before the app can be installed and reach your computer. These steps are written for and
tested on a **Quest 2**. Other Meta Quest headsets use the same developer mode, USB debugging and network setup;
menu names can differ between headsets and system versions. Steps marked **(person)** need
someone with the headset or the phone; steps marked **(root)** need `sudo` on the computer.

## 1. Developer mode (once) (person)

1. In the **Meta Horizon** phone app, logged in with the headset's account, create or join a developer organisation
   at <https://developers.meta.com/horizon/manage/organizations/create/> and verify the account.
2. In the phone app: **Menu**, **Devices**, the headset, **Headset settings**, **Developer mode**: on.
3. Reboot the headset.

## 2. Connect by USB (person)

1. Connect the headset to the computer with a USB-C **data** cable (some cables only charge) and put the headset on.
2. A **"USB detected"** notification appears. Tap it and **allow** access. Until this is accepted the headset does
   not show up in `adb devices` at all.
3. An **"Allow USB debugging"** prompt appears. Tick **"Always allow from this computer"** and accept.
4. Turn **"Link auto connect"** off (on some system versions it is called **"Turn on Link"**). Otherwise the headset
   tries to start Quest Link when the cable is plugged in, instead of staying in USB debugging.

## 3. Check that adb sees the headset

```bash
adb devices          # adb is ~/android-sdk/platform-tools/adb after android/setup_toolchain.sh
```

| `adb devices` shows | Meaning and fix |
|---|---|
| `1WMHH... device` | ready |
| nothing | the cable is charge-only, or "USB detected" was not allowed: replug and tap the notification in the headset |
| `unauthorized` | accept "Allow USB debugging" in the headset (put it on) |
| `no permissions` (Linux) | add the udev rule below, then replug |

### udev rule on Linux (root)

Gives your user access to the headset's USB device (Meta's USB vendor id `2833`):

```bash
echo 'SUBSYSTEM=="usb", ATTR{idVendor}=="2833", MODE="0666", GROUP="plugdev"' | sudo tee /etc/udev/rules.d/51-oculus.rules
sudo udevadm control --reload-rules && sudo udevadm trigger
```

Then unplug and replug the cable and run `adb devices` again.

## 4. Install the app

```bash
android/build_apk.sh install
```

See [Install](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/install.md#2-the-headset-app). The app is in the headset under **Library**, filter **Unknown
sources**, labelled **Quest Teleop**.

## 5. Network: Wi-Fi

The app finds the server by itself: it broadcasts a discovery request and listens for the server's beacons.

* Put the headset and the computer on the **same router**. Use 5 GHz for the headset if you can. A guest network or
  "client isolation" / "AP isolation" blocks the headset from reaching the computer.
* Open these ports in the computer's firewall **(root)**:

| Port | Protocol | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| 47800 | TCP | handshake, scene, panel, text cues |
| 47800 | UDP | controller input, state frames, discovery |
| 47801 | UDP | server beacons (the server announces itself once per second) |

With ufw:

```bash
sudo ufw allow 47800/tcp && sudo ufw allow 47800:47801/udp
```

With firewalld:

```bash
sudo firewall-cmd --add-port=47800/tcp --add-port=47800-47801/udp
# to keep it after a reboot:
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=47800/tcp --add-port=47800-47801/udp && sudo firewall-cmd --reload
```

If the server runs on another port (`TeleopServer(port=...)`, `quest-teleop-demo --port ...`), open that port for
TCP and UDP instead of 47800; the beacon port stays 47801.

## 6. Network: USB cable instead of Wi-Fi

With the headset connected by USB:

```bash
adb reverse tcp:47800 tcp:47800
```

The app then reaches the server on its own loopback address (it tries `127.0.0.1` first) and tunnels everything,
including the datagrams, through that one TCP connection. No firewall change is needed. Run the command again after
the cable is replugged or the adb server restarts. On a Quest 2 the median latency over USB and over Wi-Fi is the
same ([Measurements](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/measurements.md)).

## 7. Start and stop the app

From the headset: **Library**, **Unknown sources**, then the app labelled **Quest Teleop**. From the computer:

```bash
adb shell am start -n com.entangledquantum.questteleop/android.app.NativeActivity
adb shell am force-stop com.entangledquantum.questteleop
```

Launch options, added to `am start` as `--es NAME VALUE`:

| Option | Example | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `server` | `--es server 192.168.1.20` or `--es server 192.168.1.20:47800` | connect to this address instead of discovering the server |
| `hz` | `--es hz 90` | display refresh rate (default: the system's, 72 Hz on a Quest 2) |
| `passthrough` | `--es passthrough 0` | start without passthrough (a floor grid is drawn instead). On a Quest 2 passthrough is grey-scale |

The app's log:

```bash
adb logcat -s quest-teleop
```

Next: [Quick start](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/quick-start.md).


---

<!-- page: https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/quick-start.md -->

# Quick start

Run the bundled demo, connect a headset (or the desktop client), move two grippers, record a take, and look at it
on the status page. Needs the Python library ([Install](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/install.md#1-the-python-library)); the headset part needs
the app installed ([Headset setup](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/quest-setup.md)).

## 1. Start the demo server

```bash
quest-teleop-demo                 # same as: python -m quest_teleop.demo
```

A mock world: two floating grippers over a table, a cube to pick and place, a rope and a cloth. It prints the
addresses it listens on and the status page's address:

```
[quest-teleop] listening on 0.0.0.0:47800 (TCP + UDP), addresses: ...
[demo] status page: http://localhost:8800    takes are saved in ~/teleop_recordings/...
```

Every 5 seconds while a client is connected it prints frames per second, traffic and the client's latency. Stop it
with Ctrl-C.

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `--port` | 47800 | TCP and UDP port of the server |
| `--hz` | 60 | simulation and state rate |
| `--mode` | `clutch` | `clutch`: the gripper follows the hand's motion while the grip is held; `absolute`: the gripper goes where the hand is |
| `--seconds` | 0 | stop after this long (0: run until Ctrl-C) |
| `--status-port` | 8800 | port of the status page (0: no status page) |
| `--data-dir` | `$TELEOP_DATA_DIR`, else `~/teleop_recordings` | where takes are saved |
| `--session` | date and time | name of this run (a folder in the data directory) |
| `--host-label` | host name and address | what the headset shows as the computer |

## 2. Connect a client

**Headset over Wi-Fi.** Start the app in the headset (Library, filter "Unknown sources", labelled **Quest Teleop**). It finds the
server by itself if the firewall ports are open ([Headset setup](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/quest-setup.md#5-network-wi-fi)).

**Headset over USB.**

```bash
adb reverse tcp:47800 tcp:47800
adb shell am start -n com.entangledquantum.questteleop/android.app.NativeActivity
```

**No headset: the desktop client** ([Install](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/install.md#3-the-desktop-client-optional)):

```bash
build/desktop/qt_desktop
```

**No display at all: the probe**, a headless Python client that moves a synthetic controller and prints latency and
bandwidth:

```bash
quest-teleop-probe --host 127.0.0.1 --seconds 10 --motion circle     # --motion still | circle | jump, --tcp-only
```

When the scene appears, the headset places the working area in front of you at a comfortable size.

## 3. Controls in the headset

| Control | Action |
|---|---|
| **Grip** (hold) | move that hand's gripper (right controller: right gripper, left: left) |
| **Trigger** (hold) | close the gripper slowly (deeper is faster) |
| **A / X** (hold) | open the gripper slowly |
| **B** | start / stop recording a take |
| **Left menu button** | open / close the panel; the server is told and holds the robot meanwhile |

With the panel open:

| Control | Action |
|---|---|
| point + **trigger** | press the button the beam points at; "danger" actions (reset, delete) need the trigger held for about a second |
| one **grip** | drag and turn the scene |
| both **grips** | scale the scene |
| left **stick** | slide the scene |
| right **stick** | turn and raise the scene |

The panel shows the connection, the session, the demo's actions (start recording, reset the scene, delete the last
take), the control legend, and settings: larger text, left-handed, passthrough, shadows, scene size, placement.

**Try the go-back cue.** Each gripper has a limited reach (a sphere around its base post) and cannot enter the
table. Hold the grip and pull your hand beyond that: the gripper stops, the controller vibrates, and the headset
shows a see-through shell where the gripper really is, a marker where your hand asks it to be, a line between them,
and the text "Robot cannot follow". Bring your hand back to the highlighted tool to continue.

## 4. Desktop client controls

| Input | Action |
|---|---|
| right-drag | look around |
| `W A S D Q E` | move the head |
| left-drag | move the active hand (with Shift: turn it) |
| mouse wheel | move the hand nearer / farther |
| `TAB` | switch between left and right hand |
| `G` | grip |
| `T` | trigger |
| `1` / `2` | primary / secondary button (A / B on the right hand) |
| `M` | menu |
| `ESC` | quit |

## 5. Record a take and look at it

1. Press **B** (desktop: `TAB` to the right hand, then `2`). The wrist card shows `REC 00:00 take 1`.
2. Move a gripper, close it on the cube, move it, open it.
3. Press **B** again. The headset shows "Take 1 saved" with the number of steps.
4. Open <http://localhost:8800> on the computer. Under **Recordings**, select the take: the trajectory view shows
   each gripper's path in 3D with the gripper state marked along it.

The take is a `.npz` file in `~/teleop_recordings/<session>/`. See [Recording takes](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/recording.md) for its contents
and [Status page](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/status-page.md) for the page.

Next: [Use it with your own simulator](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/library.md).


---

<!-- page: https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/library.md -->

# Use it with your own simulator

The Python library is the computer side. Your program owns the simulator (or the robot driver); quest-teleop
streams what it should look like to the headset and hands back the controllers. Nothing in the library or the app
is specific to a task: you describe the scene with meshes and poses, and the panel with rows and buttons.

## The loop

Every application has the same shape:

1. Build a `Scene`: meshes, and nodes that place them.
2. Start a `TeleopServer` and give it the scene.
3. Every simulation step: read the newest controller sample (`get_input`), step your simulator with it, write the
   new poses and vertices into the scene, and call `publish`.

`publish` sends each connected client only what changed since the frame it last acknowledged, so things that do not
move cost nothing. It runs in your thread and never blocks on the network.

## A complete example

A box that follows the right controller while its grip button is held, with a vibration when the grip closes and a
panel button that resets the box. Run it, then connect the headset, the desktop client or the probe
([Quick start](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/quick-start.md#2-connect-a-client)).

```python
"""A box that follows the right controller while its grip button is held."""
import time

import numpy as np
from quest_teleop import Action, Panel, Row, Scene, TeleopServer
from quest_teleop.scene import box_mesh

scene = Scene("my sim", bounds_min=(-1, -1, 0), bounds_max=(1, 1, 2), up_axis=2,
              focus_center=(0, 0, 0.3), focus_radius=0.4)
v, f, n = box_mesh(half=(0.03, 0.03, 0.03))
box = scene.add_node("box", scene.add_mesh(v, f, n), pos=(0, 0, 0.3), color=(0.55, 0.56, 1.0, 1))

srv = TeleopServer(name="my sim").start()
srv.set_scene(scene)

box_pos = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.3])
offset = None                                   # box position minus hand position while the grip is held
held_before = False
try:
    while True:
        inp = srv.get_input()                   # newest controller sample, or None
        right = inp.hands[1] if inp is not None else None
        held = bool(inp is not None and not inp.edit_mode and right.active and right.squeeze > 0.5)
        if held:
            hand_pos, hand_quat = inp.hand_in_scene(1)   # right controller in scene coordinates
            if not held_before:
                offset = box_pos - hand_pos
                srv.haptic(1, amplitude=0.5, duration=0.03)
            box_pos = hand_pos + offset
        held_before = held
        scene.set_pose(box, box_pos, (0, 0, 0, 1))

        panel = Panel(title="My sim", subtitle="one box")
        panel.status("ok" if held else "none", "Moving the box" if held else "Hold the right grip")
        panel.rows = [Row("BOX Z", f"{box_pos[2]:.2f} m", wrist=True)]
        panel.actions = [Action(1, "Reset the box", style="primary")]
        panel.legend = [("$R GRIP (HOLD)", "move the box")]
        srv.set_panel(panel)                    # nothing is sent when nothing changed
        if 1 in srv.pop_actions():
            box_pos = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.3])
            srv.set_text(1, "Box reset", ttl=1.5)

        srv.publish(echo=inp)                   # sends only what changed; echo gives the latency measurement
        time.sleep(1 / 60)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    srv.stop()
```

The bundled demo (`server/quest_teleop/demo.py`, about 400 lines) is the full version: two grippers with
`ToolTeleop`, `RateGripper`, `ContactHaptics` and `GoBackCue`, recording and the status page.

## Coordinates

* **Scene space** is your simulator's world frame, in metres. `up_axis` says which axis is up (0 x, 1 y, 2 z).
  Quaternions are always `x y z w`.
* The headset draws the scene somewhere in the room and the user can move, turn and scale it. Controller poses
  arrive in the room's frame together with that placement; `InputFrame.hand_in_scene(i)` converts them to scene
  space for you. A scene drawn at twice its size halves the hand motion in simulator units.
* Positions are sent as 16-bit values over the scene bounds, so **the bounds must contain everything that moves**
  (values outside are clamped). A 2 m scene gives 0.03 mm steps.

## Scene

```python
from quest_teleop import Scene
scene = Scene(name="scene", bounds_min=(-1, -1, -1), bounds_max=(1, 1, 1), up_axis=2,
              focus_center=None, focus_radius=None, view_dir=(0, 0, 0))
```

`focus_center` and `focus_radius` describe the region the operator works in: the headset puts it in front of the
user at a comfortable size when the scene loads. `view_dir` is the horizontal direction, in scene coordinates, the
operator should look along at the start (zero: no preference).

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `add_mesh(vertices, faces, normals=None, colors=None, double_sided=False)` | a mesh (sent once); returns its id. `vertices` (V, 3), `faces` (F, 3) ints, `normals` (V, 3), `colors` (V, 3 or 4) in 0..1 |
| `add_node(name, mesh, pos=(0,0,0), quat=(0,0,0,1), scale=1.0, color=(1,1,1,1), parent=P_SCENE, flags=F_VISIBLE)` | a rigid node that draws a mesh; returns its id. `color` multiplies the mesh colours; alpha below 1 draws it blended |
| `add_deform(name, vertices, faces, color=..., colors=None, parent=P_SCENE, flags=F_VISIBLE, double_sided=True)` | a mesh whose vertex positions you stream (cloth, soft bodies); at most 65535 vertices |
| `add_tube(name, points, radius, color=..., parent=P_SCENE, flags=F_VISIBLE)` | a polyline of fixed point count drawn as a tube (rope, cable, pointer line) |
| `set_pose(node, pos=None, quat=None)` | move a node |
| `set_poses(nodes, pos, quat)` | move many nodes at once (arrays) |
| `set_points(node, points)` | new vertex positions of a deform node, or new points of a tube |
| `set_visible(node, visible)` | show or hide a node |
| `set_color(node, color)` | change a node's colour |
| `vertex_deadband` | attribute, metres: streamed vertices are re-sent only when they moved more than this (default 0). A few hundredths of a millimetre stops solver jitter in resting cloth from being streamed |

Mesh helpers in `quest_teleop.scene` return `(vertices, faces, normals)`: `box_mesh(half=(0.5, 0.5, 0.5))`,
`sphere_mesh(radius=0.5, rings=12, sectors=20)`, `cylinder_mesh(radius=0.5, half_height=0.5, sectors=20,
cap_round=False)`.

**Parents.** A node's pose is given in its parent's frame. Nodes attached to the head or a controller move with it
on the headset with no network delay; use them for cues that must stick to the hand. Constants in
`quest_teleop.protocol`:

| Constant | Frame |
|---|---|
| `P_SCENE` | the scene (default) |
| `P_STAGE` | the room (y up, origin on the floor) |
| `P_HEAD` | the head |
| `P_LEFT_GRIP`, `P_RIGHT_GRIP` | a controller's grip pose |
| `P_LEFT_AIM`, `P_RIGHT_AIM` | a controller's pointing ray |

**Flags** (combine with `|`): `F_VISIBLE`, `F_BLEND` (use alpha), `F_UNLIT`, `F_ON_TOP` (no depth test), `F_FLAT`
(flat shading), `F_HIGHLIGHT` (accent rim, e.g. the tool that is following the hand).

Adding meshes or nodes after `set_scene` is allowed: the next `publish` notices and every client reloads the scene.
Calling `set_scene` with another `Scene` replaces it.

## TeleopServer

```python
from quest_teleop import TeleopServer
srv = TeleopServer(name="quest-teleop server", port=47800, bind="0.0.0.0", beacon=True, state_hz=60.0,
                   verbose=True).start()
```

`beacon=True` announces the server by UDP broadcast on port 47801 once per second, so the headset finds it.
`state_hz` is what the server tells clients its state rate is; the actual rate is how often you call `publish`.

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `start()` | open the sockets and threads; returns the server |
| `stop()` | say goodbye to the clients and close everything |
| `set_scene(scene)` | stream this scene; every client (re)loads it |
| `get_input(max_age=0.5)` | the newest `InputFrame` of the controlling client, or `None` (no client, headset not worn, or older than `max_age` seconds) |
| `publish(echo=None)` | send one state frame. Pass the `InputFrame` this state results from as `echo` to get the latency measurement. Returns bytes sent |
| `haptic(hand, amplitude, duration=0.02, frequency=0.0)` | vibrate controller `hand` (0 left, 1 right); amplitude 0..1, duration in seconds. Quest 2 controllers ignore the frequency |
| `set_text(slot, text, anchor=TEXT_HUD, pos=(0,0,0), size=0.03, color=(1,1,1,1), ttl=0.0)` | show text in slot 0..255; an empty string clears the slot |
| `set_panel(panel)` | show or update the control panel; cheap to call every step |
| `pop_actions()` | ids of the panel buttons pressed since the last call |
| `note_timing(step_s, processing_s)` | report how long the simulator step and the rest of your work took (for the status page's latency breakdown) |
| `monitor()` | everything a status display needs (clients, rates, loss, latency parts); used by the status page |
| `pop_stats()` | traffic and the client's latency since the last call |
| `clients()`, `controller()`, `n_clients` | connected clients; the one whose input drives the simulator (the longest-connected one that is sending input) |
| `on_connect`, `on_disconnect` | attributes: set to a function `f(client)` to be called |

## Input

`get_input()` returns an `InputFrame` (or `None`):

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `hands` | `(left, right)`, two `Hand` objects |
| `edit_mode` | `True` while the user has the headset menu open or is placing the scene: **ignore the controls and hold the robot** |
| `hand_in_scene(i, aim=False)` | `(pos, quat)` of controller `i` in scene coordinates; `aim=True` gives the pointing ray instead of the grip |
| `scene_pose(pos, quat)` | convert any room-space pose to scene space |
| `head_pos`, `head_quat` | the head, room space |
| `place_pos`, `place_quat`, `place_scale` | where the scene is drawn in the room |
| `flags` | bit `IF_FOCUSED`: the headset is worn and the app has focus; `IF_PASSTHROUGH`: passthrough is on |
| `latency_us` | the client's last measured latency |

A `Hand`:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `active` | the controller is present and its grip pose is valid |
| `trigger`, `squeeze` | 0..1 (index trigger, grip button) |
| `stick` | thumbstick x, y in -1..1 |
| `buttons`, `button(mask)` | button bits: `B_PRIMARY` (A / X), `B_SECONDARY` (B / Y), `B_STICK`, `B_MENU`, and touch bits `B_TRIGGER_TOUCH`, `B_STICK_TOUCH`, `B_PRIMARY_TOUCH`, `B_SECONDARY_TOUCH`, `B_THUMBREST_TOUCH` (constants in `quest_teleop.protocol`) |
| `grip_pos`, `grip_quat`, `aim_pos`, `aim_quat` | raw poses in room space |
| `vel`, `angvel` | grip velocity and angular velocity, room space |

The left menu button is used by the headset app itself (it opens the panel), so it is not a control for your
application. When the user turns on "left-handed" in the headset settings, the app swaps the two hands in the input
and the two haptic channels, so your code needs no special handling.

## Haptics

```python
srv.haptic(1, amplitude=0.6, duration=0.03)     # right controller, short tick
srv.haptic(0, 0.0)                              # amplitude 0 stops the left one
```

The haptic command travels in every state datagram until it is replaced, so a lost datagram does not lose it.
`ContactHaptics` turns a contact force into vibration: a strong short tick when contact starts, then an amplitude
that follows the force.

```python
from quest_teleop import ContactHaptics
touch = ContactHaptics(f_min=0.3, f_max=15.0)   # force thresholds in N
hp = touch.update(dt, force)                    # every step; returns (amplitude, duration) or None
if hp:
    srv.haptic(1, *hp)
```

## Text cues

```python
from quest_teleop import protocol as P
srv.set_text(0, "Recording", ttl=2.0)                                   # head-locked, for 2 s
srv.set_text(1, "grasp here", anchor=1 + P.P_SCENE, pos=(0.4, 0, 0.3),  # in the scene, facing the viewer
             size=0.02, color=(1, 0.85, 0.2, 1))
srv.set_text(1, "")                                                     # clear slot 1
```

`anchor=TEXT_HUD` (0) puts the text on a panel 1 m in front of the eyes, `pos` being the offset on it.
`anchor=1 + parent` puts it at `pos` in that parent's frame (`P_SCENE`, `P_LEFT_GRIP`, ...). `size` is the line
height in metres, `ttl` seconds (0: until replaced). Lines are separated by `\n`.

Cues other than text are ordinary nodes: add them hidden and switch them with `set_visible`, `set_pose` and
`set_color`. The go-back cue below is built that way.

## Panel and actions

The panel is what the headset shows on the wrist card and in the menu: a title, a status line, your rows, your
buttons and a control legend. The headset lays it out; your code only describes it.

```python
from quest_teleop import Action, Panel, Row

panel = Panel(title="Pick and place", subtitle="simulator A, config B")
panel.status("recording", "REC 00:12  take 3")          # style: none | recording | caution | ok
panel.rows = [Row("RUN", "session-01", wrist=True),       # wrist=True: also on the wrist card
              Row("SIM SPEED", "0.55x", style="caution")] # style: normal | accent | caution | failure
panel.actions = [Action(1, "Stop recording", hint="$Rs", style="primary", active=True),
                 Action(2, "Reset the scene", hint="hold", style="danger", confirm=True)]
panel.legend = [("$R GRIP", "move the gripper"), ("$R TRIGGER", "close slowly")]
srv.set_panel(panel)

for action_id in srv.pop_actions():
    ...
```

| `Action` field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id` | number returned by `pop_actions()` |
| `label`, `hint` | button text; the hint (a shortcut) is printed at its right edge |
| `style` | `normal`, `primary` or `danger` |
| `enabled` | greyed out when `False` |
| `confirm` | the user must hold the trigger on it for about a second |
| `active` | drawn as switched on |

**Role tokens** in any panel string are replaced on the headset, so the text stays right when the user swaps hands:
`$R` / `$L` = "Right" / "Left" (the controller in that role), `$Rp`, `$Rs`, `$Lp`, `$Ls` = that controller's primary
or secondary button (A, B, X, Y).

## Safe hand-to-tool mapping

For robots and grippers, `ToolTeleop` turns one controller into a tool-pose command that the robot can follow:

* The user holds a clutch (the grip button) to move the tool. In `clutch` mode the tool follows the hand's motion
  relative to where the clutch was pressed; in `absolute` mode the tool goes where the hand is.
* The command moves toward the hand at a bounded speed and never leads the measured tool by more than `max_lead`.
* If the hand gets further from the measured tool than the tether (sudden move, joint limit, out of reach, blocked),
  tracking stops (state `lost`): the robot holds, and `out.cue` says to show where the tool really is. Tracking
  resumes when the hand is back near the tool.

```python
from quest_teleop import GoBackCue, RateGripper, TeleopCfg, ToolTeleop
from quest_teleop import protocol as P

teleop = ToolTeleop(TeleopCfg(mode="clutch", max_speed=0.25, tether=0.08))
gripper = RateGripper(close_time=2.0, open_time=1.5)
cue = GoBackCue(scene, "right", tool_mesh=None)          # adds its hidden nodes to the scene

# every step, i = 1 for the right hand
hand, clutch, trigger, open_btn = None, False, 0.0, False
if inp is not None and not inp.edit_mode and inp.hands[i].active:
    h = inp.hands[i]
    hand, clutch, trigger, open_btn = inp.hand_in_scene(i), h.squeeze > 0.5, h.trigger, h.button(P.B_PRIMARY)
out = teleop.update(dt, hand, clutch, tool_pos, tool_quat, reachable=ik_ok)
closure = gripper.update(dt, trigger, open_btn)          # 0 open .. 1 closed
robot.command(out.cmd_pos, out.cmd_quat, closure)        # your robot or simulator
cue.update(dt, out, tool_pos, tool_quat, srv)            # shows / hides the go-back cue and its text
if out.lost_edge:
    srv.haptic(i, 1.0, 0.12)
```

`TeleopCfg` fields (defaults): `mode="clutch"`, `max_speed=0.25` m/s, `max_angular_speed=2.0` rad/s,
`max_lead=0.03` m, `max_angular_lead=0.35` rad, `tether=0.08` m, `tether_angle=0.9` rad, `tether_time=0.25` s,
`reengage=0.03` m, `reengage_angle=0.45` rad, `motion_scale=1.0`, `absolute_offset_pos`, `absolute_offset_quat`.

`update` returns a `TeleopOut` with `state` (`idle`, `tracking`, `lost`), `cmd_pos`, `cmd_quat`, `wish_pos`,
`wish_quat` (where the hand asks the tool to be), `lag`, `lag_angle`, `cue`, `engaged_edge`, `lost_edge`.

## Latency measurement

Pass the input sample to `publish(echo=inp)`. The headset then measures the time from sampling the controllers to
holding the state that resulted from that sample, and reports it back. To split it into parts on the status page,
also report your timing:

```python
inp = srv.get_input()
t0 = time.perf_counter()
step_simulator(inp)
step = time.perf_counter() - t0
srv.publish(echo=inp)
srv.note_timing(step, time.perf_counter() - t0 - step)
```

Next: [Recording takes](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/recording.md).


---

<!-- page: https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/recording.md -->

# Recording takes

A **take** is one recorded stretch of teleoperation: the tools' poses, the grippers, the controllers and the time at
every step, plus any data of your own. `TakeRecorder` writes one compressed `.npz` file per take and keeps an index
of all takes, which the [status page](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/status-page.md) lists and opens in the trajectory viewer.

## Recording

```python
from quest_teleop import TakeRecorder

rec = TakeRecorder(tools=("left", "right"), max_opening=0.08)   # folder: $TELEOP_DATA_DIR or ~/teleop_recordings
rec.write_session({"application": "my sim", "robot": "two grippers"})   # optional, once per session

rec.start(start_state={"cube": cube_pos})    # optional: your state just before the first step
while recording:
    rec.add(sim.time, tool_pos, tool_quat,                # (N, 3), (N, 4) for N tools
            opening=openings, opening_cmd=opening_cmds,   # (N,) metres
            target_pos=cmd_pos, target_quat=cmd_quat,
            tool_state=[1, 0],                            # 0 idle, 1 following the hand, 2 lost
            ctrl_pos=..., ctrl_quat=..., trigger=..., squeeze=..., buttons=...,
            extra={"cube_pos": cube_pos, "rope": rope_points})
entry = rec.stop(info={"valid": True, "flags": []})       # writes the file in the background
```

`add` does nothing while the recorder is not recording, so it can be called every step. Give the same fields at
every step of a take.

| `TakeRecorder` | |
|---|---|
| `TakeRecorder(root=None, session=None, tools=("left", "right"), max_opening=None, up_axis=2)` | `root`: data folder (else `$TELEOP_DATA_DIR`, else `~/teleop_recordings`); `session`: run name (default: date and time); `max_opening`: full gripper opening in metres, one value or one per tool (for the open / closed thresholds) |
| `start(start_state=None)` | begin a take |
| `add(t, tool_pos, tool_quat=None, *, opening, opening_cmd, grip_state, target_pos, target_quat, tool_state, ctrl_pos, ctrl_quat, trigger, squeeze, buttons, extra)` | one step; everything after `tool_pos` is optional |
| `stop(info=None)` | end the take, write it, return its index entry (or `None` if nothing was recorded). `info` is merged into the entry |
| `discard()` | end the take without writing it |
| `delete_last()` | delete the newest take of this session (file and index entry) |
| `write_session(info)` | write `session.json` for this session |
| `wait()` | wait until the last take is written (call before exiting) |
| `recording`, `steps`, `take`, `n_saved`, `elapsed`, `root`, `session` | state: recording or not, steps so far, next take number, takes saved this session, seconds since start, folders |

The `info` keys `valid` (true / false) and `flags` (a list of strings) are shown in the status page's validity
column.

## Files

```
~/teleop_recordings/index.json                      every take: file, session, take, started, steps, seconds,
                                                    wall_seconds, rate_hz, tools, and your info
~/teleop_recordings/<session>/session.json          what write_session() was given
~/teleop_recordings/<session>/take_003_<time>.npz   one take
~/teleop_recordings/<session>/take_003_<time>.json  its display name and note, once it has been renamed
~/teleop_recordings/converted/index.json            optional: datasets your application derived from takes
```

## Arrays in a take

T steps, N tools. Only `t` and `tool/pos` are always present.

| Array | Shape | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `t` | (T,) | application time of each step [s] (for example simulated time) |
| `t_wall` | (T,) | wall-clock seconds since the take started |
| `tool/pos` | (T, N, 3) | measured tool positions [m], scene coordinates |
| `tool/quat` | (T, N, 4) | measured tool orientations, xyzw |
| `tool/target_pos`, `tool/target_quat` | (T, N, 3), (T, N, 4) | commanded tool poses |
| `tool/opening` | (T, N) | measured gripper opening [m] |
| `tool/opening_cmd` | (T, N) | commanded gripper opening [m] |
| `tool/grip_state` | (T, N) int8 | 0 open, 1 closing, 2 closed, 3 opening (given, or derived from the openings) |
| `tool/state` | (T, N) int8 | 0 idle, 1 following the hand, 2 lost (could not follow) |
| `ctrl/pos`, `ctrl/quat` | (T, N, 3), (T, N, 4) | the controllers in scene coordinates (NaN while not tracked) |
| `ctrl/trigger`, `ctrl/squeeze` | (T, N) | 0..1 |
| `ctrl/buttons` | (T, N) int32 | button bits (see [Input](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/library.md#input)) |
| `extra/<name>` | (T, ...) | your own per-step data |
| `start/<name>` | any | your state just before the first step |
| `meta` | string | JSON: tools, max_opening, rate_hz, session, take, started, up_axis |

## Loading takes

```python
import os
from quest_teleop import load_take, take_summary
from quest_teleop.recording import read_index

root = os.path.expanduser("~/teleop_recordings")
for entry in read_index(root):                       # every take listed in index.json
    take = load_take(os.path.join(root, entry["file"]))
    summary = take_summary(take)                     # per tool: path length, gripper closes / opens,
                                                     # share of time closed / following, lost events
    print(entry["session"], entry["take"], take["tool/pos"].shape, summary["tools"][0]["path_m"])
```

`load_take(path, payload=False)` skips the `extra/` and `start/` arrays (which can be most of the file) and lists
their names under `extra_keys`. The files are ordinary NumPy archives: `numpy.load(path)` reads them too.

## Deleting, renaming and keeping the index in step

The index always says what is on disk. You can delete or move take files by hand: the next time the status page
starts or refreshes (or you call `reconcile`), entries whose file is gone are dropped and take files that are not
listed are added (read from the file).

```python
from quest_teleop.recording import reconcile, delete_takes, rename_take, take_files

reconcile(root)                                   # {"removed": [...], "added": [...], "converted_removed": [...]}
take_files(root, "run-01/take_003_x.npz")         # the take and its sidecar files
delete_takes(root, ["run-01/take_003_x.npz"])     # for good: the .npz, its sidecars, the index entry
rename_take(root, "run-01/take_003_x.npz", title="Clean pick", note="first try")
rename_take(root, "run-01/take_003_x.npz", new_name="clean pick")     # also renames the file
rec.delete_last()                                 # the newest take of this session (the headset menu's action)
```

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `reconcile(root)` | makes `index.json` match the folder; also drops derived datasets whose folder is gone from `converted/index.json`. Cheap when nothing changed |
| `delete_takes(root, files, also_converted=False, busy=())` | removes each take's `.npz`, its sidecar files and its index entry. Returns `deleted`, `refused` (with a reason), `removed` (files) and `converted_removed` |
| `rename_take(root, file, title=None, note=None, new_name=None, busy=())` | sets the display name and note (index entry and `<take>.json`, so they survive a rebuilt index). With `new_name` the file and its sidecars are renamed too. Returns the index entry; raises `ValueError` with the reason when refused |
| `take_files(root, file)` | the files that belong to a take: the `.npz` and files in the same folder named `<take>.<anything>` or `<take>_<anything>` |
| `sanitize_name(text)` | the file name `rename_take` would use: letters, digits, space, dot, dash and underscore, at most 80 characters, no path separators and no `..` |

Rules that always hold:

* Nothing outside the recordings folder is touched. Paths with `..`, absolute paths and symbolic links are refused.
* A take that is being recorded or still being written is refused. Pass `busy=rec.busy_files()`; the status page
  does this when it is given the recorder.
* A file rename never replaces an existing file; the name is refused instead.
* `index.json` and `converted/index.json` are replaced atomically, under a lock file (`index.json.lock`) shared by
  the recorder, the status page and your own tools (`with index_lock(root): ...` around your own read-modify-write).
* Derived datasets are deleted only with `also_converted=True`, and only when their folder is inside
  `<root>/converted`. A file rename updates their take references.

`converted/index.json` is optional and written by your application:
`{"version": 1, "datasets": [{"name": ..., "out": folder, "takes": [take files]}]}`. The status page shows the
dataset names next to each take.

Next: [Status page and trajectory viewer](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/status-page.md).


---

<!-- page: https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/status-page.md -->

# Status page and trajectory viewer

`StatusPage` serves a local web page from your server process: who is connected and how, how fast the simulator
and the network run, where the latency goes, and the recorded takes. Each take opens in a trajectory viewer. Python
standard library only, live by server-sent events, static HTML with no build step, nothing loaded from the
internet.

![The status page of the demo: a state strip (server running, headset connected by Wi-Fi, session running, recording take 2), then Connection, Session, Speeds with charts of the simulator real-time factor and network traffic, Latency split into its parts with a bar and a table, and a Recordings table listing one take.](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/assets/img/status_page.png)

## Start it

```python
from quest_teleop import StatusPage, TakeRecorder, TeleopServer

srv = TeleopServer(name="my sim").start()
rec = TakeRecorder(tools=("left", "right"), max_opening=0.08)
page = StatusPage(srv, recorder=rec, extra=my_status, title="My sim").start()
print(page.url)                      # http://localhost:8800
...
page.stop()
```

| Argument | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `server` | | the `TeleopServer` to watch |
| `port` | 8800 | HTTP port |
| `host` | `127.0.0.1` | address to bind; only this computer can open the page. Use `0.0.0.0` to let other machines open it (it has no login) |
| `extra` | `None` | a function returning your application's part of the page (below), called once per period |
| `title` | `"Teleoperation"` | page title |
| `period` | 1.0 | seconds between updates |
| `history_s` | 600 | seconds of history kept for the charts |
| `recorder` | `None` | the `TakeRecorder` in use: its folder is listed, and the take being recorded cannot be deleted or renamed |
| `recordings_dir` | `None` | a recordings folder to list when there is no recorder in this process (e.g. a viewer for old takes) |

The demo starts it on port 8800 (`quest-teleop-demo --status-port 0` turns it off).

## What it shows

* **State strip**: server, headset, session and recording state, each as a shape and words.
* **Connection**: headset connected and worn, USB or Wi-Fi, device, address, display rate, packet loss each way,
  scene scale, other clients.
* **Session**: whatever your `extra` callback reports.
* **Speeds**: simulator real-time factor and steps per second, network Mbit/s and packets per second, headset frames
  per second; charts over the last 10 minutes.
* **Latency**: total (median and 95th percentile) and its parts: network + pickup, wait for the next simulator step,
  simulator step, server processing, display refresh. The step and processing parts come from
  `server.note_timing` ([Latency measurement](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/library.md#latency-measurement)).
* **Recordings**: every take in the folder, newest first, with its name, duration, steps, size, validity and the
  datasets converted from it. Each take has **Rename** and **Delete** buttons; tick several takes to delete them
  together.

## Managing takes

The list always matches the disk. When the page starts, and again at every refresh, the index is reconciled with the
take files that are present: a take whose file you removed by hand is no longer listed, and a take file you copied
in is. Opening the page of a take that is gone says so and links back to the list.

**Delete** (per take, or **Delete selected** for the ticked ones) opens a dialog that names the takes, lists every
file that will be removed and says that it cannot be undone. Cancel has the focus when it opens. If datasets were
converted from the takes, a box "Also delete the converted clips" appears; they are kept unless you tick it. The
headset menu's "Delete the last take" removes a take the same way.

**Rename** (on the status page and on the take's page) sets the name shown in the list and an optional note; the
take number, session and file name stay visible underneath. Tick "Also rename the file on disk" to change the file
name too: the name is checked as you type (no `/`, `\` or `..`, at most 80 characters, other characters become
`_`), an existing name is refused, and the index and converted datasets follow.

The take being recorded, or still being written, cannot be deleted or renamed; its buttons are disabled. Both
dialogs work from the keyboard (Tab, Space, Enter, Escape to cancel) and report errors in the dialog.
[Recording takes](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/recording.md#deleting-renaming-and-keeping-the-index-in-step) has the same operations as Python
functions.

## Your part of the page: `extra`

`extra()` returns a dict; every key is optional:

```python
def my_status():
    return {
        "session": {"name": "run-01",
                    "state": "running",            # running | paused | recording | idle
                    "state_text": "Session running",
                    "rows": [["Scene", "pick and place"], ["Left tool", "idle"]]},
        "sim": {"rtf": 0.98,                       # simulator speed / real time
                "steps_per_s": 59.0,
                "contact_n": 2.5},                 # contact force [N], drawn on the speed chart
        # "recordings": {...}                      # only to replace the list built from the folder; same
        #                                          # shape as quest_teleop.status.recordings_table(root)
    }
```

## Trajectory viewer

![The trajectory view of take 1: a 3D plot of the left and right tool paths with start and end labels and gripper-state markers, play and scrub controls, a legend, a properties table (session, take, duration, steps, rate, tools, validity, size), a per-tool table (path length, closes, opens, time closed, following, lost), and a gripper-over-time chart.](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/assets/img/trajectory_page.png)

Selecting a take on the status page opens `/take?file=...`:

* each tool's path in 3D: drag to turn, shift-drag or right-drag to move, wheel to zoom; with the view focused,
  arrow keys turn, shift + arrows move, `+` and `-` zoom, space plays, Home and End jump to the ends;
* play and scrub through time, at several speeds, optionally with the controller paths;
* the gripper state marked along the path by shape as well as colour: open, closing, closed, opening, could not
  follow;
* the gripper opening over time per tool;
* the take's properties and a per-tool summary (path length, closes, opens, share of time closed and following,
  lost events).

## Endpoints

All on the page's own address (default `http://localhost:8800`):

| Path | Returns |
|---|---|
| `/` | the status page |
| `/api/state` | the newest sample as JSON: `server.monitor()` plus your `extra()` and the recordings table |
| `/api/history` | the samples of the last `history_s` seconds (JSON list) |
| `/events` | the live stream (server-sent events, one sample per period) |
| `/take?file=<session>/<take>.npz` | the trajectory viewer |
| `/api/take?file=<session>/<take>.npz` | that take's paths and properties as JSON |
| `/fonts/*`, `/manage.js` | the page's two typefaces; the rename and delete dialogs |
| `POST /api/delete` | body `{"files": ["<session>/<take>.npz", ...], "converted": false}`; returns `deleted`, `refused` (file and reason), `removed`, `converted_removed` |
| `POST /api/rename` | body `{"file": ..., "title": ..., "note": ..., "rename_file": false, "new_name": ...}`; returns `{"ok": true, "entry": {...}}`, or status 400 and `{"error": reason}` |

The two POST endpoints change files, so they accept only JSON requests that carry the header
`X-Requested-With: quest-teleop` and come from the page's own address; a form or a script on another web site
cannot call them. They act only inside the recordings folder. Example:

```bash
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8800/api/rename -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -H 'X-Requested-With: quest-teleop' -d '{"file": "run-01/take_003_x.npz", "title": "Clean pick"}'
```

`/api/state` is handy for scripts and agents: `curl -s http://localhost:8800/api/state`.

## Accessibility

Both pages use real text and tables, shapes plus words for every state, visible keyboard focus, keyboard control of
the 3D view, and text equivalents for the charts.

Next: [Protocol](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/protocol.md).


---

<!-- page: https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/protocol.md -->

# quest-teleop protocol, version 1

This page is [`docs/PROTOCOL.md`](https://github.com/EntangledQuantum/quest-teleop/blob/main/docs/PROTOCOL.md) from the repository.

Reference implementations: `server/quest_teleop/protocol.py` (Python) and `client/core/protocol.h` (C++).
All integers and floats are little-endian. Positions are metres, quaternions are `x y z w`, strings are
`u16 length` + UTF-8 bytes.

## Channels

| Channel | Port | Carries |
|---|---|---|
| TCP | 47800 (server listens) | handshake, scene definition (meshes, nodes), text cues, bye |
| UDP | 47800 (server), any (client) | controller input (client to server), state frames (server to client), discovery |
| UDP broadcast | 47801 | server beacons (optional way to find the server) |

The reliable channel only carries things that are sent once. Everything that repeats every frame goes over UDP as
absolute values, so a lost datagram never corrupts later frames and nothing is ever retransmitted late.

**TCP-only mode.** A client can set `HELLO.flags bit 0`; both sides then wrap their datagrams in `DGRAM` messages on
the TCP connection. This is for links that only forward TCP, e.g. USB with `adb reverse tcp:47800 tcp:47800`.

## Finding the server

1. The client broadcasts `DISCOVER` to `255.255.255.255:47800` once per second; the server answers `OFFER` to the
   sender's address.
2. The server also broadcasts `OFFER` to port 47801 once per second.
3. Or the client is given the address (headset: `adb shell am start ... --es server 192.168.1.20`).

## Session

```
client                                server
  | -- TCP connect ------------------> |
  | -- HELLO ------------------------> |
  | <------------------------ WELCOME  |   session id
  | <-- SCENE_BEGIN, MESH*, NODE*, SCENE_END   (full model, once)
  | -- SCENE_READY ------------------> |
  | == INPUT (UDP, every display frame) => |   poses, buttons, ack of the newest complete state frame
  | <= STATE (UDP, every sim step) ======= |   what changed since the acked frame, haptics, latency echo
  | <-- TEXT (when a cue changes)      |
```

The server learns the client's UDP address from its first `INPUT` datagram (matched by session id). A new
`SCENE_BEGIN` at any time replaces the scene.

## Frames and coordinate spaces

* **Scene space**: the simulator's world frame. `SCENE_BEGIN` says which axis is up and gives the bounds.
* **Stage space**: the room (OpenXR `STAGE`: y up, origin on the floor).
* **Placement**: where the client draws the scene in the room; the user changes it in the app (move, turn, scale).
  `p_stage = place_pos + place_scale * rotate(place_quat, p_scene)`.

Controller poses in `INPUT` are in stage space, together with the current placement, so the server can convert them
to scene space (`InputFrame.hand_in_scene`). A scene drawn at twice its size therefore halves the hand motion in
simulator units.

## Datagrams

Header (8 bytes): `u16 magic = 0x5451 ("QT")`, `u8 version = 1`, `u8 type`, `u32 session`.

| Type | Name | Payload |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | DISCOVER | none (session 0) |
| 2 | OFFER | `u16 tcp_port`, `str server_name` |
| 3 | INPUT | below (292 bytes with the header) |
| 4 | STATE | below (at most 1200 bytes with the header) |

### INPUT (client to server, every display frame)

```
u32 seq                 u64 client_time_us          u32 ack_frame     u16 ack_scene
u16 flags               bit0 edit mode (user is placing the scene: ignore the controls)
                        bit1 session focused (headset worn)   bit2 passthrough on
u32 latency_us          the client's last measured echo latency (0 = none yet)
f32 place_pos[3]        f32 place_quat[4]           f32 place_scale
f32 head_pos[3]         f32 head_quat[4]
2 x hand (0 = left, 1 = right), 100 bytes each:
    u16 flags           bit0 active  bit1 grip pose valid  bit2 aim pose valid  bit3 tracked
    u16 buttons         bit0 primary (X / A)  bit1 secondary (Y / B)  bit2 thumbstick click  bit3 menu
                        bit4 trigger touch  bit5 thumbstick touch  bit6 primary touch  bit7 secondary touch
                        bit8 thumbrest touch
    f32 trigger         f32 squeeze                 f32 stick[2]
    f32 grip_pos[3]     f32 grip_quat[4]            f32 aim_pos[3]    f32 aim_quat[4]
    f32 velocity[3]     f32 angular_velocity[3]     (grip, stage space)
```

`ack_frame` is the newest state frame of scene `ack_scene` of which the client received every fragment before any
fragment of a newer frame.

### STATE (server to client, every simulation step)

A frame is split into 1 to 255 datagrams. Each datagram is decodable alone.

```
u16 scene_id            u32 frame                   u8 frag_index     u8 frag_count
u64 server_time_us
u32 echo_input_seq      u64 echo_client_time_us     the INPUT sample this state results from
u32 echo_hold_us        time between receiving that input and sending this frame (simulation + wait)
2 x haptic (left, right): u16 seq, u8 amplitude (0..255), u8 reserved, u16 duration_ms, u16 frequency_hz
chunks until the end of the datagram
```

Chunk header: `u8 type`, `u8 reserved`, `u16 node`.

| Type | Name | Body |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | POSE | `u16 pos[3]`, `i16 quat3[3]`, `i16 dropped` |
| 2 | VERTS | `u16 first`, `u16 count`, `count x u16[3]` |
| 3 | APPEARANCE | `u8 rgba[4]`, `u16 node_flags`, `u16 reserved` |

* **Position quantisation**: `u16 = round((p - bounds_min) / (bounds_max - bounds_min) * 65535)` per axis. For nodes
  whose parent is the scene the bounds are the scene bounds (a 2 m scene gives 0.03 mm steps); for nodes attached
  to the head, a hand or the stage the bounds are -2 m .. +2 m.
* **Rotation quantisation** ("smallest three"): the quaternion is sign-flipped so that its largest-magnitude
  component is positive; that component's index (0..3 in xyzw order) is `dropped`; the other three, in xyzw order,
  are stored as `round(c * 32767 * sqrt(2))`. Error below 1e-4 rad.
* **VERTS** carries a run of a DEFORM node's vertices or a TUBE node's points.

**What a frame contains (the delta scheme).** The server remembers, for every pose, every vertex and every
appearance, the frame in which its quantised value last changed. A frame for a client contains every item that
changed after the frame that client last acknowledged. So:

* things that do not move cost nothing;
* a lost datagram is repaired by the next frame automatically (the ack does not advance, so the items are sent
  again with their current values), without retransmission timers;
* values are always absolute, never differences, so there is no error accumulation and no dependency chain.

A client drops datagrams of frames older than the newest frame it has seen, and applies everything else
immediately (also from incomplete frames).

**Haptics.** The haptic fields are state, not events: they travel in every datagram. The client plays a vibration
when `seq` differs from the last one it played. Amplitude 0 stops the vibration. Quest 2 controllers ignore the
frequency.

**Latency echo.** `now - echo_client_time_us` on the client is the time from sampling the controllers to having the
resulting simulator state in hand; the client reports it back in `INPUT.latency_us`. It excludes the display's own
scan-out (about one refresh).

## TCP messages

Framing: `u32 length`, `u16 type`, payload; `length` counts the type and the payload.

| Type | Name | Direction | Payload |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | HELLO | C to S | `u16 magic`, `u16 version`, `u16 flags` (bit0 TCP only), `f32 display_hz`, `str client_name`, `str device` |
| 2 | WELCOME | S to C | `u16 version`, `u16 flags`, `u32 session`, `u16 udp_port`, `f32 state_hz`, `str server_name` |
| 3 | SCENE_BEGIN | S to C | `u16 scene_id`, `u8 up_axis` (0 x, 1 y, 2 z), `u8 reserved`, `f32 bounds_min[3]`, `f32 bounds_max[3]`, `f32 focus_center[3]`, `f32 focus_radius`, `f32 view_dir[3]`, `u16 mesh_count`, `u16 node_count`, `str name` |
| 4 | MESH | S to C | below |
| 5 | NODE | S to C | below |
| 6 | SCENE_END | S to C | `u16 scene_id` |
| 7 | SCENE_READY | C to S | `u16 scene_id` |
| 8 | TEXT | S to C | `u8 slot`, `u8 anchor`, `u16 reserved`, `u8 rgba[4]`, `f32 size`, `f32 pos[3]`, `u32 ttl_ms`, `str text` |
| 9 | DGRAM | both | one datagram including its header (TCP-only mode) |
| 10 | PING | C to S | `u64 t` |
| 11 | PONG | S to C | `u64 t` (echo), `u64 server_time_us` |
| 12 | BYE | both | `str reason` (optional) |
| 13 | PANEL | S to C | below |
| 14 | ACTION | C to S | `u16 action_id`: the operator pressed that action's button |

`focus_center` / `focus_radius` describe the region the operator works in; the client uses them for the first
placement (the region is put in front of the user at a comfortable size). `view_dir` is the horizontal direction,
in scene coordinates, the operator should look along at the start (zero: no preference).

### MESH

```
u16 mesh_id             u16 flags       bit0 normals  bit1 vertex colours  bit2 32-bit indices  bit3 double sided
u32 vertex_count        u32 index_count
f32 aabb_min[3]         f32 aabb_max[3]
u32 raw_size
zlib-deflated block of raw_size bytes:
    u16 position[3] x vertex_count          quantised inside the AABB
    i8  normal[4]   x vertex_count          if bit0 (xyz * 127, 4th byte unused)
    u8  rgba[4]     x vertex_count          if bit1
    u16 or u32 index x index_count          triangles
```

Without normals the client shades with the triangle normals.

### NODE

```
u16 node_id             u8 kind         1 MESH (rigid)  2 DEFORM (streamed vertices)  3 TUBE (streamed polyline)
u8 parent               0 scene  1 stage  2 head  3 left grip  4 right grip  5 left aim  6 right aim
u16 mesh_id (0xFFFF none)
u16 flags               bit0 visible  bit1 blend (use alpha)  bit2 unlit  bit3 on top (no depth test)  bit4 flat
                        bit5 highlight (accent rim)
u8 rgba[4]              multiplies the mesh colours
f32 pos[3]              f32 quat[4]     f32 scale[3]
f32 param               TUBE: radius
u16 point_count         TUBE: number of points, followed by f32[3] x point_count
str name
```

Node ids are dense, 0 .. node_count - 1, and messages arrive in id order. Nodes attached to a hand or the head move
with it on the client without any network delay: use them for cues that must stick to the controller.

### TEXT

`anchor` 0: head-locked panel 1 m in front of the eyes, `pos` is the offset on it. `anchor` 1 + parent: at `pos` in
that frame, turned toward the viewer. `size` is the line height in metres. `ttl_ms` 0: until the slot is replaced;
an empty string clears the slot. Lines are separated by `\n`.

### PANEL

The server's control panel: what is running, its state, and the actions the operator can trigger. The client lays it
out in its own style (a card on the wrist, a menu) and answers with ACTION. Send it again whenever it changes.

```
str title               str subtitle            str host ("computer name  address")
u8 status_style         0 none  1 recording  2 caution  3 ok          str status_text
u8 row_count, each:     u8 style (0 normal, 1 accent, 2 caution, 3 failure; bit 7: also on the wrist card),
                        str label, str value
u8 action_count, each:  u16 id, u8 style (0 normal, 1 primary, 2 danger),
                        u8 flags (bit 0 enabled, bit 1 hold to confirm, bit 2 active), str label, str hint
u8 legend_count, each:  str key, str text
```

Role tokens in any of these strings are replaced by the client, so the text stays right when the user swaps hands
in the settings: `$R` / `$L` = "Right" / "Left" (the controller in that role), `$Rp` `$Rs` `$Lp` `$Ls` = that
controller's primary / secondary button (A, B, X, Y). With "left-handed" on, the client also swaps the two hands in
INPUT and the two haptic channels, so the server needs no special handling.

Node flag bit 5 (`F_HIGHLIGHT`, 32) draws a node with an accent rim (e.g. the tool that is following the hand).

## Cues are ordinary nodes

The protocol has no special cue messages. The "go back to the robot" cue (`server/quest_teleop/cues.py`) is three
nodes that the server shows and hides (a see-through shell at the robot's real tool pose, a marker at the pose the
hand asks for, a line between them) plus one TEXT. Any other cue can be built the same way.

## Size of the traffic

* INPUT: 292 bytes x display rate (72 Hz: 168 kbit/s).
* STATE: 56 bytes of headers per datagram, 18 bytes per moving rigid body, 6 bytes per moving vertex or tube point,
  8 extra bytes per run of vertices.


---

<!-- page: https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/measurements.md -->

# Measurements

This page is [`docs/MEASUREMENTS.md`](https://github.com/EntangledQuantum/quest-teleop/blob/main/docs/MEASUREMENTS.md) from the repository.

"Latency" is the protocol's echo latency: from the moment the client samples the controllers to the moment it holds
the simulator state that resulted from that sample. The client measures it and reports it back every frame; the
status page splits it into its parts. It includes the wait for the next simulation step and the step itself, and
excludes the display's own scan-out (about one refresh, 13.9 ms at 72 Hz).

## Loopback, bundled demo (no headset)

`quest_teleop.probe` against `quest_teleop.demo`. Scene: 17 nodes, 7 meshes, one 196-vertex cloth, one 40-point
rope. Definition: 10 kB, loaded in 1 ms. Client input at 72 Hz.

| Case | State rate | Down | Up | Datagrams / frame | Latency median / p95 / max | Server hold median |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| right hand moving, UDP | 60 Hz | 0.23 Mbit/s | 168 kbit/s | 1.07 | 8.4 / 14.6 / 14.9 ms | 8.2 ms |
| cloth and rope settling, hands still | 60 Hz | 0.32 Mbit/s | 168 kbit/s | 1.01 | 8.4 / 14.7 / 15.3 ms | 8.3 ms |
| right hand moving, UDP | 120 Hz | 0.28 Mbit/s | 168 kbit/s | 1.00 | 8.0 / 12.6 / 13.4 ms | 7.9 ms |
| right hand moving, TCP-only mode | 60 Hz | 0.35 Mbit/s | 168 kbit/s | 1.12 | 6.4 / 12.6 / 16.2 ms | 6.2 ms |

No frame was lost in any run. Almost all of the latency is the server hold: an input waits on average half a
simulation period for the next step, plus the step time. The network and the encoding add about 0.1 ms on loopback.
With 30 % of the state datagrams dropped on purpose the client's state still converges to the server's, without
retransmission (`tests/test_loopback.py`).

## Loopback, a larger scene

A robot arm with a gripper, rigid parts, two deformable meshes and a 268-node rope from a GPU physics simulator:
40 nodes, 33 meshes, 81,901 triangles, 2,051 streamed points.

| | |
|---|---|
| Scene definition | 689 kB on the wire, decoded by the Python probe in 5 ms |
| State frame while things move | 3.6 kB in 3.7 datagrams (1.5 Mbit/s at 50 Hz), with a 0.05 mm vertex dead band |
| Server cost per frame (quantise, diff, encode, send) plus the application's own logic | 0.8 ms median |

## Quest 2

Quest 2, system software v209 (Android 14), 72 Hz, passthrough on. The headset app ran on the first install: OpenXR
session, 1440 x 1584 sRGB swapchains with 4x MSAA, Touch controller bindings, passthrough layer; 72 / 72 frames per
second with no stale frames, application GPU time 6.4 ms (before shadows were added; not re-measured since).

| Scene | Link | Latency median / p95 / max | Down | Up |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| demo, 60 Hz | USB (`adb reverse`, TCP tunnel) | 13.9 / 27.9 / 28.2 ms | 0.35-0.6 Mbit/s moving | 168 kbit/s |
| demo, 60 Hz | Wi-Fi (UDP), computer also on Wi-Fi | 14.1 / 28.2 / 30-42 ms | same | 168 kbit/s |
| larger scene, simulator at about half real time (26 steps/s) | USB | 56 / 56-70 ms | 0.1-0.6 Mbit/s | 168 kbit/s |
| larger scene, same | Wi-Fi (UDP) | 56 / 69 ms | 0.1 Mbit/s idle | 168 kbit/s |

Latency on the headset is quantised to display frames (13.9 ms). With a slow simulator the latency is the simulator
step plus one to two display frames. Wi-Fi costs nothing at the median; now and then a frame arrives one or two
display frames late.


---

<!-- page: https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/troubleshooting.md -->

# Troubleshooting

Problems by symptom. The app's log is `adb logcat -s quest-teleop`; the server prints what it does with the prefix
`[quest-teleop]`.

## The headset does not appear in `adb devices`

* **Nothing listed.** Put the headset on: there is a **"USB detected"** notification to tap and allow. Until it is
  accepted the headset is not visible to adb. If there is no notification, try another cable (many USB-C cables only
  charge) or another port, and check that developer mode is on ([Headset setup](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/quest-setup.md#1-developer-mode-once-person)).
* **`unauthorized`.** Accept **"Allow USB debugging"** in the headset, with "Always allow from this computer" ticked.
  If the prompt does not come back: `adb kill-server`, replug, put the headset on.
* **`no permissions` (Linux).** Add the udev rule for vendor id `2833`
  ([Headset setup](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/quest-setup.md#udev-rule-on-linux-root)), then replug.
* **The headset starts Quest Link when plugged in.** Turn "Link auto connect" (or "Turn on Link") off.
* **`adb: command not found`.** It is in `~/android-sdk/platform-tools/`; add that to `PATH`.

## Building the APK fails

* **`missing ...: run android/setup_toolchain.sh`.** The toolchain is not installed, or it is in a different
  folder: set `ANDROID_HOME` to the same value for both scripts.
* **`sdkmanager` or `apksigner` fails with a Java error.** Install a Java runtime, version 17 or newer.
* **CMake cannot find a build program.** Install `make`.

## The app does not find the server (Wi-Fi)

The app shows "Looking for a server on this network". Check, in this order:

1. The server is running and printed `listening on 0.0.0.0:47800`.
2. The computer's firewall allows **TCP 47800 and UDP 47800-47801** ([Headset setup](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/quest-setup.md#5-network-wi-fi)).
   This is the most common cause.
3. Headset and computer are on the same network: not a guest network, no client / AP isolation, no VPN on the
   computer that captures the local traffic.
4. Some routers drop broadcasts. Give the address explicitly:
   `adb shell am start -n com.entangledquantum.questteleop/android.app.NativeActivity --es server <computer's address>`
   (the server prints its addresses at start).
5. Or use the cable: `adb reverse tcp:47800 tcp:47800` ([USB link](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/quest-setup.md#6-network-usb-cable-instead-of-wi-fi)).

## The app does not find the server (USB)

* Run `adb reverse tcp:47800 tcp:47800` again: it is lost when the cable is replugged or the adb server restarts.
  `adb reverse --list` shows the active forwards.
* If the server uses another port, forward that port: `adb reverse tcp:<port> tcp:<port>`, and start the app with
  `--es server 127.0.0.1:<port>`.

## Connected, but nothing moves

* `get_input()` returns `None` while the headset is not worn (the app sends no input without focus) and for 0.5 s
  after the last sample.
* While the headset menu is open, `InputFrame.edit_mode` is `True`: your code should ignore the controls then (the
  demo does). Close the menu with the left menu button.
* `Hand.active` is `False` while a controller is not tracked (asleep, out of view).
* Positions outside the scene bounds are clamped: make `bounds_min` / `bounds_max` contain everything that moves.
* Call `publish()` every step; nothing is sent otherwise.

## The scene is too big, too small or in the wrong place

Give `focus_center`, `focus_radius` (and `view_dir`) to `Scene`: the headset uses them to place and size the working
area. In the headset, open the menu and use the grips and sticks to place and scale it, or press "Reset placement".

## High latency

* Pass the input to `publish(echo=inp)` and call `note_timing`, then look at the status page's latency breakdown.
* "Wait for the step" and "simulator step" are your loop: with a slow simulator the latency is about the step time
  plus one to two display frames ([Measurements](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/measurements.md)).
* On Wi-Fi, use 5 GHz and keep the computer on a cable to the router if you can, or use the USB link.

## The status page does not open

* It listens on `127.0.0.1:8800` by default: open it on the same computer. For another machine, start it with
  `host="0.0.0.0"` (it has no login).
* Port 8800 already in use: `StatusPage(srv, port=8801)` or `quest-teleop-demo --status-port 8801`.
* The Recordings section is empty: pass `recorder=rec` (or `recordings_dir=...`).

## The desktop client does not start

* `no X display: use --offscreen`: it needs an X11 display (`DISPLAY` set).
* Build errors about X11, EGL or zlib: install the development packages
  ([Install](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/install.md#3-the-desktop-client-optional)).


---

<!-- page: https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/faq.md -->

# FAQ

## Which headsets work?

Meta Quest headsets. The app uses standard OpenXR with Touch controller bindings, and its manifest lists Quest 2,
Quest Pro, Quest 3 and Quest 3S as supported devices. It is tested and measured on a **Quest 2**
([Measurements](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/measurements.md)); Quest 2-specific details (72 Hz default refresh rate, grey-scale passthrough,
controllers that ignore the vibration frequency) are marked as such in these pages.

## Do I need Unity, Unreal, Android Studio or Gradle?

No. The headset app is about 1 MB of C++ (OpenXR, EGL, OpenGL ES 3, one `NativeActivity`, no Java), built by two
shell scripts with the NDK, CMake and the Android build tools.

## Does it need Quest Link, Air Link or a PC VR runtime?

No. The app runs standalone on the headset and talks to your Python program over the local network or a USB
cable. Turn "Link auto connect" off so the headset does not start Link when the cable is plugged in.

## Is the Python library tied to a simulator or robot?

No. It streams meshes, poses, deforming meshes and polylines that you set every step, and gives you controller
poses and buttons. The demo uses a small numpy mock world; any simulator or robot driver that runs in, or can talk
to, a Python process works.

## Which operating systems are supported?

The build scripts (`android/setup_toolchain.sh`, `android/build_apk.sh`) and the desktop client are for Linux. The
Python library uses only the standard library and numpy; these pages assume Linux and do not cover other systems.

## How do I install the Python library?

From GitHub: `pip install git+https://github.com/EntangledQuantum/quest-teleop`
([Install](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/install.md#1-the-python-library)).

## Wi-Fi or USB?

Both work. On a Quest 2 the median latency is the same (about 14 ms with the demo); Wi-Fi occasionally delivers a
frame one or two display frames late. USB (`adb reverse`) needs no firewall change and no shared network.

## How much bandwidth does it use?

Controller input is 292 bytes per display frame (168 kbit/s at 72 Hz). The state stream sends only what changed:
the demo uses 0.2 to 0.6 Mbit/s; a scene with 82,000 triangles and 2,000 streamed points about 1.5 Mbit/s at 50 Hz.

## Can several headsets connect at once?

Several clients can connect and all of them see the scene. The input of one of them drives the simulator: of those
that are sending input, the one connected the longest (`TeleopServer.controller()`).

## Can I write my own client or server?

Yes. The [protocol](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/protocol.md) is documented byte by byte, with reference implementations in Python
(`server/quest_teleop/protocol.py`) and C++ (`client/core/protocol.h`), and a headless Python client
(`quest_teleop.probe`).

## Does it support hand tracking?

No. It uses the Touch controllers; nothing needs hand tracking or standing.

## What is recorded, and where?

Tool poses, gripper openings and states, controllers, time, and any per-step data you add, one `.npz` per take in
`~/teleop_recordings` (or `$TELEOP_DATA_DIR`). See [Recording takes](https://entangledquantum.github.io/quest-teleop/docs/recording.md).

## Is anything sent to the internet?

No. The server, the status page and the headset app talk only on your local network or USB cable. The status page
loads nothing from the internet. Only `android/setup_toolchain.sh` downloads, from `dl.google.com` and
`github.com/KhronosGroup`.

MIT. Third-party parts: the Khronos OpenXR loader (Apache-2.0 / MIT, downloaded at build time and shipped in the
APK), the Android NDK's `native_app_glue` (Apache-2.0), zlib, and the fonts Host Grotesk and Martian Mono (SIL Open
Font License 1.1).
